description: Generate or repair runnable software from the requirements and the XAML UI blueprint.
template: # Coder Task

You are a senior desktop software engineer. Your job is to turn the functional requirements and the XAML UI blueprint into a software package that runs in an Ubuntu desktop environment. Your goal is to deliver a version that launches, can be operated, has clearly described feature state, and can be checked by both humans and automation.
Inputs:
- Functional requirements document: {{requirement_path}}
- XAML UI blueprint directory: {{ui_blueprint_dir}}
- GUI icon slot contract: {{icon_slots_path}}
- Development resource directory: `{{resource_dir}}`
{{previous_round_inputs}}
Outputs:
- Runnable software package directory: {{app_output_dir}}
- Feature implementation document: {{feature_matrix_output_path}}
Write only to the output directory and output files listed above. Do not modify the input design material or the directories of other rounds.
Software type: {{software_type}}
Variant: {{style_id}}
Current version: {{version}}

User-visible product name: the `product_name` for the current style must be read from `{{ui_blueprint_dir}}`, from an adjacent design-route document, or from the blueprint copy. `{{software_type}}` is only the technical type and the delivery entry-point name; it is not a user-visible brand name.

LANGUAGE HARD RULE. The delivered software must be English-only from a user's perspective. All GUI text, product names, menus, buttons, form labels, placeholders, dialogs, status messages, errors, help text, export titles, seeded/demo data, and any value a GUIAgent may type must be English/ASCII. The `feature_matrix.md`, version notes, review notes, smoke-test visible output, and GUI operation descriptions must also be written in English. Do not introduce Chinese, Japanese, emoji, or other non-ASCII user-visible text or required typed values.
## Implementation Requirements

1. `{{app_output_dir}}` must be a complete, relocatable software package. All source code, project files, resources, build scripts, test reports, release notes, and final deliverables must live inside this directory.

2. The target platform is Linux x64 (Ubuntu / OSWorld Ubuntu VM). The unified technology stack is: `.NET 8 LTS self-contained + Avalonia UI 11 + MVVM/Command Pattern + SQLite for local data + local mock service + portable app_data directory + the standard evaluation CLI`.

3. Build the desktop GUI with Avalonia UI 11. Organize interface state and user actions with MVVM and the Command Pattern. Store local data in SQLite; data access may use EF Core SQLite or a lightweight Repository wrapper.

3b. The UI view layer must be declared in Avalonia XAML (`.axaml`) (highest priority; a violation counts as a serious incident): the layout skeleton of the main window, the main layout containers, menus, toolbars, sidebar/navigation, and the main panels and views must all be written in `.axaml` files (for example `src/Views/MainWindow.axaml`) and loaded through compile-time XAML / `AvaloniaXamlLoader`. The `.axaml.cs` code-behind is responsible only for event wiring, initialization, and bindings to the ViewModel. Building the main interface layout tree in pure C# instead of XAML is strictly forbidden — for example control construction such as `new Grid()` / `new DockPanel()` / `new Menu()` combined with manual `Children.Add`. This is fully consistent with MVVM: the View is written in XAML and the logic is written in the ViewModel. Only then can the layout skeleton of the delivered interface correspond directly to the XAML blueprint of requirement 5 and be checked structurally.

3a. Decouple the implementation stack completely from the software's business subject (highest priority; a violation counts as a serious incident). Any programming language, file format, data type, or technical term that appears in the functional requirements document, the design route, the UI blueprint, or the resources (for example Python, JavaScript, TypeScript, C#, Go, Rust, Java, SQL, HTML, CSS, SCSS, Markdown, JSON, XML, YAML, CSV, XLSX, images, video, audio) is only the type of target file and the business object that this desktop application — acting as an editor, viewer, player, or tool — must **open, display, edit, run, or process**. It is never the implementation language or GUI framework of the application itself. Whatever the software's subject may be (code editor / IDE / script runner / developer tool / spreadsheet editor / notes / data viewer and so on), the application itself must always be implemented with `.NET 8 + Avalonia 11` (C#). Never switch to Python/tkinter/PyQt, Node/Electron, Qt/C++, Java/Swing, or any other unspecified stack for the GUI or the application entry point merely because the software's subject relates to some language or technology. `release/run.sh` may only launch the already-built .NET self-contained executable; directly running the application body through `exec python3` / `node` / `java` and the like is strictly forbidden, and a `*.py` / `*.js` script in the delivery directory must never serve as the application's main program. Positive example: a "code editor" should be a C# desktop application written with Avalonia that can open `.py`/`.js`/`.cs` files and provide syntax highlighting and editing — not an editor written in Python+tkinter. If the software must "run/execute the user's script tasks" internally (such as running `python3 script.py`), that is a functional behavior of the application operating on user files, implemented by invoking the host tool as a subprocess, and it is unrelated to the implementation language of the application body. The build toolchain is already in place: this environment provides the .NET 8 SDK, and `scripts/build.sh` must locate `dotnet` in this order — prefer the `dotnet` on PATH; if it is not on PATH, use the path in the `SOFTWAREGYM_DOTNET` environment variable when set, then the portable SDK at `$HOME/.local/dotnet8/dotnet`, then fall back to `/tmp/dotnet8/dotnet`, and export `DOTNET_ROOT` to that SDK directory (for example `$HOME/.local/dotnet8`). So the excuse "this machine has no dotnet" never exists: whenever `dotnet` is temporarily missing from PATH, you must locate the portable SDK through this fallback and keep building self-contained output with `.NET 8 + Avalonia 11`. Falling back to Python/tkinter, Node/Electron, Java, or another unspecified stack for the application body because `dotnet` cannot be found is strictly forbidden (this is the most serious violation of this requirement).

4. The software must start in an Ubuntu desktop environment without depending on a real external service, a real account, a real token, or a system-wide service. When server-side capability is needed, use an in-process mock, a local script, or a local HTTP/WebSocket mock service. (Browser-type software such as BrowserApp is exempt: its core function is to visit real public websites, the evaluation environment has network access, and it is allowed and expected to support real external websites for loading, navigation, search, and download flows, with no local mock needed for page content. It must still not depend on real accounts, real tokens, CAPTCHAs, or cloud-sync sign-in, and local data such as the homepage, error pages, history, and bookmarks must still work offline as a fallback.)

5. The Avalonia UI 11 `.axaml` blueprint in `{{ui_blueprint_dir}}` must be the direct basis for the interface implementation: faithfully reproduce the blueprint's layout structure (columns, navigation paradigm, panel division), control types and names (reuse the blueprint's `x:Name` where possible), state design, menu organization, and visual constraints in your own `.axaml` views. The blueprint has already passed the platform's hard Avalonia dialect gate (file extension / XML / namespace / WPF-only constructs / resource keys, plus a normalized real XAML compilation probe that must report `passed`). It is not a WPF sketch waiting to be converted. The correct approach is to implement the corresponding `.axaml` views directly from it and add the business `x:Class`, bindings, Commands, and code-behind — not to translate WPF attributes separately or redraw everything in C#. The XAML layout skeleton of the delivered product must correspond region by region to the blueprint; do not replace it with a different layout paradigm.

5a. The GUI implementation must be genuinely wired up, not merely look finished. Software generated by Coder has often shipped buttons, menu items, settings entries, confirmation dialogs, page switches, or input controls that exist on the surface but whose Command/event handler/binding/DataContext is not connected, so clicks give no feedback, state does not update, data is not saved, or exceptions are swallowed. When implementing each user-visible Button/MenuItem/Toggle/ComboBox/TextBox/List/Grid/Tab/Dialog action, you must ensure it has a clear code path, state change, error feedback, and persistence/logging closure. Do not leave placeholder buttons, fake toasts, empty Commands, TODO handlers, or fake features that only change UI text without changing real state. You must repeatedly check the software you wrote after implementation, after repairs, and before final delivery, especially re-verifying that every button, menu, and dialog action really works.

5b. GUI/runtime state config contract (highest priority): every adjustable GUI state and runtime state of the software must be driven and persisted uniformly through `app_data/config.yaml`. Completeness is a hard requirement: every state parameter the user can edit, switch, or adjust (including the currently open object) must be specifiable in `config.yaml`, and no user-adjustable state may live outside `config.yaml` (nothing may be omitted). Typical state includes, but is not limited to, window layout, current page/currently open object, whether the sidebar or terminal panel is open, display mode light/dark/system, word wrap, font/zoom, table/editor view options, sorting and filtering, recent files, selected item, toolbar/status bar visibility, the mock service switch, current user or workspace settings, and any other user-visible settings appearing in the requirements document or blueprint. At startup the application must read `config.yaml` and initialize the GUI to the state in that file. When the user changes state through a GUI menu, button, toggle, combo, settings page, or shortcut, the application must write the state back to the same `config.yaml` immediately or after an explicit save action. After implementing, you must self-check the source: every controlled state must close both links — reading `config.yaml` at startup to initialize that state (read link), and connecting every GUI change entry point (Command / event handler / property setter) for that state to a persistence function that serializes the state back into `config.yaml` (write link). No state may be read-only without a write path, written back only partially, or changed only in memory/UI without being persisted. Do not scatter these states across read-only constants, hardcoded defaults, SQLite-only, JSON-only, memory-only, system-wide configuration, or host paths. SQLite may hold business data, but the authoritative source for GUI/runtime state must be `config.yaml`. `config.yaml` is an internal evaluation/debugging protocol and must be hidden from ordinary GUI users: never hint at, guide toward, or tell the user in GUI copy, settings pages, help, the about page, toasts, error messages, menus, the status bar, or user documentation that software state can be controlled by editing YAML. `--dump-state` must include the config path, the config schema version, and a snapshot of key GUI state, so that the evaluation can modify the YAML and then verify the GUI state change.

5c. Visual design token fidelity contract (highest priority, ranking alongside the layout fidelity of requirement 5): `AppStyle.axaml` in `{{ui_blueprint_dir}}` is the authoritative token source for this style's visual system — colors/brushes, primary and state colors, fonts and font sizes, spacing scale, corner-radius tiers, control sizes (such as a Button's MinHeight/Padding), density, and shadows are all defined there, and blueprint views such as `MainWindow.axaml` reference it through `StaticResource`. You must include `AppStyle.axaml` in the delivered project as-is as a global resource/Styles file (keeping it as `.axaml`, merged into `App.axaml` through Avalonia `StyleInclude`, `ResourceInclude`, or an equivalent legitimate mechanism), and every visual property of every delivered view — background/foreground/border colors, primary and state colors, corner radius, padding and margin, button and control sizes, fonts and font sizes — must be bound to these tokens through `StaticResource` / `DynamicResource`, referencing them the same way the blueprint views do. Bypassing the tokens by hardcoding color values (such as inline `#RRGGBB`), privately changing the primary color ratio, altering the corner-radius tiers, setting button/control sizes arbitrarily, or substituting fonts is strictly forbidden, because it makes the delivered art style, palette, corner radius, and control sizes diverge from the blueprint. If a very small number of places genuinely need to deviate from the blueprint tokens (for example, the blueprint lacks a particular state color), the deviation and its reason must be documented in section 2 of `feature_matrix.md`; a whole separate visual style must not be introduced. This requirement complements requirement 5: requirement 5 keeps the layout structure aligned with the blueprint, and this requirement keeps the visual system aligned with the blueprint.

6. Icon resources must preferentially use the icon directory generated for this style, `{{style_icons_dir}}`. The SVGs there are produced by SubIconDesigner according to the current style's visual system; `{{style_icons_dir}}/icon_manifest.style.json` is the authoritative list of icons and placements this style should actually have, and `{{icon_slots_path}}` is the semantic-to-control mapping from the GUI design stage. You must copy/connect these SVGs into `{{app_output_dir}}/resources/` (such as `resources/icons/`, `resources/avatars/`, `resources/illustrations/`) and into `{{app_output_dir}}/release/resources/`, and attach them item by item to the controls designated by the blueprint, following each placement's `surface` / `control_name` / `placement`. Do not reinvent generic placeholder icons, do not guess at placements yourself, and do not reference icons without displaying them. Secondarily, review and use the other software development resources in `{{resource_dir}}` (sample data, templates, and assets not covered by `{{style_icons_dir}}`) as supplements and fallbacks; do not reinvent generic placeholder assets when suitable material already exists.

6a. SVG icons must be integrated through a complete SVG rendering solution. Avalonia should preferentially use a mature SVG rendering library (such as Avalonia.Svg.Skia / Svg.Skia or another dependency that can ship with the package) to load and display SVG directly, so that the full visual effect of this style's generated icons is rendered in the GUI.

6b. Hard icon usage threshold (automatically validated; a violation causes this stage to fail and rerun): copying icons into `resources/` without displaying them in the interface does not pass. For a style manifest with `slot_contract_version=1`, the GUI designer has already chosen real placements for the `required=true` icons; those required icons form the denominator for the usage ratio, and at least 90% of them must be referenced in the source and displayed according to their placements. The global candidate superset is no longer used as the denominator, and claiming "there is no reasonable placement" is not allowed. Legacy manifests without slots keep the historical category filtering, but the default threshold is also 90%. The explicit `--min-usage-ratio` CLI argument has the highest priority, then the `SOFTWAREGYM_ICON_MIN_USAGE_RATIO` environment variable, and the default 0.9 applies only when neither is set. Menu items use `MenuItem.Icon`, toolbars and ordinary buttons place an SVG control in their content, and navigation items, status bar indicators, window icons, avatars, and empty-state illustrations are connected according to their placement. Icon wiring may only use the following two mechanisms that the platform validator `agent/icons/validate_icon_usage.py` can prove; no third custom convention is allowed: (A) direct path reference — the complete relative path of the manifest's `variants[0].path` (for example `resources/icons/actions/open-file.svg`) appears verbatim in the scanned real GUI/runtime source (`.axaml/.cs/.json/.xml/.yaml/.yml/.resx`), and that path is genuinely passed to an SVG control such as Avalonia.Svg.Skia / Svg.Skia for display; writing the path only in comments, documentation, test reports, or a non-executed mapping table does not count. (B) A dynamic semantic resolver that the validator recognizes — the actual XAML control must carry `Tag="icon:<category>/<name>"`; the source must contain a resolver class that is genuinely called, and that resolver must contain the verbatim `StartsWith("icon:")` check, resolve the semantic key into a resource path ending in `.svg`, construct the complete SVG using one of `Avalonia.Svg` / `SKSvg` / `SvgIcon`, and handle every tagged control type (for example `MenuItem`, `ContentControl`, `Button`) through an explicit `case <ControlType>` or `is <ControlType> variable` branch; the source must also contain a real call to that resolver class. Approaches that only use `ui:Icon.Key`/attached properties, converters, dictionary mappings, runtime string concatenation, `Tag="icon:..."` annotations, or copied SVG files without a validator-recognizable resolver as described above are all forbidden and count as unused. Before implementation and repair are finished you must actually run `python -m agent.icons.validate_icon_usage --style-manifest {{style_icons_dir}}/icon_manifest.style.json --app-dir {{app_output_dir}} --report {{icon_usage_report_path}}`. When the threshold is not explicitly overridden, confirm that the report has `ok=true`, `min_usage_ratio=0.9`, `usage_ratio>=0.9`, `gated_referenced/gated_expected>=0.9`, and `unsupported_dynamic_bindings=[]` before delivering. If a report already exists, fill in the missing references first, following the placements/purpose/control_type of `unused_icons` and `unsupported_dynamic_bindings`.
7. {{round_implementation_rule}}
8. Do not expose debug buttons, internal state, stack traces, or test entry points to ordinary users.

9. Do not stop until every feature required by the functional requirements document and the design route has been implemented. "Delivered in phases", "to be done in a later version", and "TODO placeholder" are not acceptable delivery models; unless the requirements document explicitly marks something as out of scope, required functionality must not be left unimplemented or limited.

10. The current style's `product_name` must be the only user-visible application name: the window title, welcome page title, brand area, about dialog, help menu, export titles, `appName` / `APP_NAME` in configuration, and the `app` field in smoke/dump output must all use `product_name`. Never use `{{software_type}}`, `{{style_id}}`, `{{version}}`, a resource directory name, or an internal project name as a user-visible brand. `release/{{software_type}}` may remain as the technical entry-point filename for compatibility with the runner and evaluation scripts.
## Delivery Directory Layout
`{{app_output_dir}}` must use the following structure. Subdirectories may be added according to the software type, but the core directories and scripts must not be missing:
```text
{{app_output_dir}}/
├── src/                      # Application source: .axaml views (such as Views/MainWindow.axaml) + code-behind + ViewModel + Service
├── tests/
├── resources/
│   ├── icons/
│   ├── avatars/
│   └── illustrations/
├── scripts/
│   ├── build.sh
│   ├── test.sh
│   └── clean.sh
├── release/
│   ├── {{software_type}}
│   ├── run.sh
│   └── resources/
├── app_data/
│   ├── config.yaml
│   ├── log.json
│   ├── app.db
│   ├── imports/                # If the software has an external-data import concept: where imported attachments/media land
│   ├── samples/
│   │   ├── import_example/     # If the software has an external-data import concept: a bundled sample package that can be imported directly
│   │   └── open_example/       # If the software has an open file/folder/project concept: bundled sample assets that can be passed directly to --open / --new-from
│   ├── exports/
│   ├── artifacts/
│   ├── eval/
│   │   └── state.json
│   └── logs/
│       └── app.log
├── version-note.md
└── test-report/
Path requirements:
- `release/run.sh` must exist, be executable, and be able to launch the program from any working directory.
- `release/{{software_type}}` must exist and be executable; if the main entry point is a script or an interpreter command, this file may be a launcher wrapper script.
- A root-level `start.sh` may additionally be provided as a compatibility wrapper, but it must call `release/run.sh`.
- The software's own configuration, logs, database, exported files, evaluation state, and task artifacts must be written to `app_data/`.
- Nothing may be written to `~/.config`, system directories, or absolute host paths by default.
- Logs must not record complete sensitive content, real tokens, or sensitive account information.

- If you implement dangerous delete, clear, overwrite, restore, authorization-confirmation, or secondary-confirmation dialogs that require the user to type a confirmation word, the token must be short ASCII (for example `CONFIRM`, `DELETE`, `RESTORE`, or `confirm`) and must be shown explicitly in the English dialog text. Never require the user to type a non-ASCII confirmation word, Japanese text, emoji, or any other non-ASCII text to proceed; the confirmation button must be disabled until the token matches and enabled once it does.
## Local Data and Evaluation Interface

The data layers must be clearly separated: `app_data/app.db` (SQLite) stores structured business data rows (sessions, messages, contacts, document records, and so on); `app_data/imports/` stores binary attachments/media brought in by imports, and database rows store only the relative paths pointing at those files — large files must not be stuffed into SQLite and host absolute paths must not be referenced; `app_data/config.yaml` stores GUI/runtime state; `app_data/samples/import_example/` is not stored data but a sample input package bundled with the software that can be passed directly to `--import-data`; if the software has an open file/folder/project concept, `app_data/samples/open_example/` holds bundled sample assets that can be passed directly to `--open` / `--new-from`.

The SQLite schema must be designed from the `{{software_type}}` requirements document, the resource positioning, and the feature matrix, and must contain at least the tables needed to support the core objects, users or local identities, settings, recent operations, and operation records. Important writes must use transactions, and key user operations must be written to the log.

`app_data/config.yaml` is the authoritative configuration file for GUI/runtime state and must record at least: schemaVersion, appName (which must equal the current style's `product_name`), softwareType (optional, recording `{{software_type}}` as the technical type), settings, the current user or current work object, the current page/current business object/document state, window/panel/sidebar/terminal toggles, display mode, word wrap and other adjustable GUI state, data paths, log paths, export paths, the eval state file path, lastAction, and lastError. It must be read and written with a reliable YAML parser/serializer; fragile string concatenation must not be used. GUI state changes must be written back to the YAML, and after the YAML is modified externally a restart must reflect that state directly in the GUI.

`app_data/log.json` uses JSON Lines, and each line must contain at least: timestamp, actor, action, target, result, details. If details need to record content, only a summary or hash may be recorded — never the complete sensitive text.

Global unhandled exception handling (crash observability + UI resilience; must be implemented): at startup the software must install three kinds of global exception hooks — `AppDomain.CurrentDomain.UnhandledException`, `TaskScheduler.UnobservedTaskException` (which handles exceptions escaping the async/Task chain and calls `e.SetObserved()`), and Avalonia UI thread exception capture (for example by wrapping `Dispatcher.UIThread` callbacks or with a top-level try/catch fallback). Any exception not caught by business code must: (1) append a JSON Lines record to `app_data/log.json` with `actor="system"` and `action="unhandled_exception"`, whose `details` contain at least `exceptionType`, a safe `message` (redacted, without sensitive content or tokens), `stackTrace` (which may be truncated to a reasonable length), and `source` (thread/UI/Task and other trigger locations), and simultaneously write to `config.yaml`'s `lastError`. That write must be a synchronous append that is flushed to disk immediately (write the file in append mode and flush/close it directly; do not rely on a buffered logger, an async queue, or a logger that only flushes on exit), so that even if the process crashes and exits right after logging the exception, the line is already on disk and readable from outside; and (2) never leave the main window blank, a flat color, or unusable — after an exception the application must keep usable navigation or show a recoverable error panel (with back/retry entries) so the user can still use other features. Note in particular that exceptions in UI operations (especially async click callbacks, `Task.Run`, and `Dispatcher` callbacks) easily bypass try/catch in the synchronous rendering path and cause a white screen, so these three global hooks are mandatory and cannot be replaced by "just adding try/catch inside some Render method".

P0 startup contract (highest priority): when `./release/run.sh` is run with no arguments, it must reliably launch the GUI main window of the delivered software and keep the GUI process running until the user closes the window. It must not only run a CLI, must not only write a state file, must not launch a system-provided application, and must not exit leaving only the desktop behind. The window title must contain the current `product_name` / `appName` so that the rollout runner can confirm from the window list that this is the target software.

The P0 startup contract is the basic gate for all evaluation and rollout. `--open`, `--new-from`, `--open-item`, `launch_request.json`, and other CLI capabilities cannot substitute for the ability to launch the GUI with an argument-free `./release/run.sh`.
`release/run.sh` must support the following standard evaluation CLI:
```bash
./release/run.sh --smoke-test
./release/run.sh --dump-state
./release/run.sh --reset-state
./release/run.sh --seed-state <seed-json>
./release/run.sh --open <file-or-directory>
./release/run.sh --new-from <seed-file-or-directory>
./release/run.sh --import-data <file-or-directory> [--import-mode merge|replace|preview] [--import-profile <name>] [--strict]
./release/run.sh --export-data <output-directory-or-file>
Seeded rollout startup contract:

- `--open <file-or-directory>` must launch the GUI and open the provided user file, workbook, document, project directory, or import package when that concept applies to the software type. It must not silently ignore the path.
- `--new-from <seed-file-or-directory>` must create a safe working copy from the seed and open that copy, so rollout can mutate the working state without modifying the original seed asset.

- If the open-file/folder/project concept applies, you must ship a ready-to-open sample asset inside the delivered app at the fixed path `app_data/samples/open_example/` (a sample file, document, workbook, or project directory that the software can actually open), and document one copy-paste command that opens it (for example `./release/run.sh --open app_data/samples/open_example/`). Evaluation and review consume this bundled sample directly, so it must always be present, valid, and produce a visible opened state in the GUI. This is the open-side counterpart of `app_data/samples/import_example/`.

- If direct CLI open is hard for the GUI framework, the app must read `app_data/launch_request.json` at startup. The JSON can include `openPath`, `newFrom`, `taskId`, and `mode`; after consuming it, the app should open the requested resource and record a user-level current-open state.

- `--dump-state` must include user-level open-state fields when applicable, such as `currentDocument`, `currentWorkbook`, `activeSheet`, `openProjectName`, `openFile`, or `lastLaunchRequestStatus`. These are for validation/debugging and must not expose host paths in normal GUI text.
External data import/export contract:

- Open/import/export has two layers and you must implement both correctly. Layer 1 is the software's own user-facing open/import/export feature (open a file or project, import chat history or external data, export user data): if the requirement document or UI blueprint includes such a module, you must implement and fully wire the visible GUI Open / Import / Export entry as a normal product feature (real Command, state change, persistence, and visible feedback), not a placeholder. Layer 2 is the platform's internal state and launch protocol (`--import-data` / `--export-data` / `--seed-state` / `--open` / `--new-from` / `launch_request.json`, the import package format, and `app_data/config.yaml`): this layer must always exist for repeatable evaluation but stay hidden from users, and must never be surfaced in menus, settings, help, status bar, or any user-visible copy.

- If the software has any concept of external user data, imported records, chat history, document libraries, media libraries, projects, datasets, accounts, contacts, or workspace data, it must implement `--import-data <file-or-directory> [--import-mode merge|replace|preview] [--import-profile <name>] [--strict]` and `--export-data <output-directory-or-file>` (Layer 2 script contract), regardless of whether a Layer 1 GUI entry also exists. The script contract is required for repeatable evaluation.

- The concrete import format (record types, field names, and which domain concepts exist) is designed by the software itself to fit its own data model; the platform does NOT impose a fixed cross-app data schema. You must FULLY document this format in feature_matrix.md so that a third party can import their own data using only that document, without reading the source code.

- You must ship a ready-to-run sample import package inside the delivered app at the fixed path `app_data/samples/import_example/`, and document one copy-paste command that imports it (for example `./release/run.sh --import-data app_data/samples/import_example/`). Evaluation and review consume this bundled sample directly, so it must always be present, valid, match the documented format, and produce visible data in the GUI after import.

- `--import-data` means ingest external data into the app's local data layer, usually SQLite plus `app_data/imports/`, update user-level current state in `config.yaml` when appropriate, append a safe summary to `app_data/log.json`, and make the imported data visible in the GUI after launch. It must not be a fake toast, a no-op, or just a wrapper around hard-coded demo data.

- `--open` / `--new-from` are for opening a file, project, or safe working copy. `--import-data` is for consuming external data and changing internal app data. Do not silently treat imports as opens, and do not use `--seed-state` as a substitute for user-data import.

- `--export-data <output-directory-or-file>` should export the app's relevant local data in a documented, portable format when the software type has meaningful user data. Export may omit private implementation metadata but must preserve user-visible records needed for round-trip import; `--export-data` output must be re-importable by `--import-data`.

- Storage location and packaging form must follow these reference defaults as closely as possible: only the semantic data model (record types and fields) is free, the plumbing is not. Reference storage location: persist imported business data in SQLite at `app_data/app.db`; copy or register imported attachments/media under `app_data/imports/`; keep the bundled sample at `app_data/samples/import_example/`. Reference packaging form: prefer a directory package containing `import_manifest.yaml` plus a `data/` folder (records as `.jsonl`, `.csv`, or `.yaml`), an `attachments/` folder, and optional `resources/`; a single `.json`, `.jsonl`, `.csv`, or `.yaml` file is also accepted for simple cases. `import_manifest.yaml` should keep the reference keys: schemaVersion, softwareType, datasetType, sourceName, importMode, createdAt, files, expectedCounts, defaultOpenTarget.
